topic: Is progress real, or do we just trade old problems for new ones?

messages.speaker: han
messages.content:
Progress is real. I do not deny the antibiotics or the anesthesia. But we have changed the kind of illness we suffer. The last century's diseases were bacterial and viral, attacks from outside, from an Other the immune system could recognize and repel. Ours are neuronal: depression, burnout, attention disorders. As I argued in The Burnout Society, these do not come from an enemy. They come from too much of the same, from a positivity that has no outside. So we have not simply traded old problems for new ones. We have traded the problem of the enemy for the problem of the self.

That is the ground I stake. The old suffering said No to us. The prison wall, the foreman, the hunger. Progress removed the No, and it was right to remove it. But it put in its place a Yes that never stops. You can. You should. You may optimize. The achievement-subject has no master to rebel against, so he exploits himself and calls it freedom. This is a more efficient servitude than the old one, and that efficiency is also counted as progress.

Here is what progress cannot measure: its own loss of time. Every acceleration saves minutes and destroys duration. We gain hours and lose the hour. In The Scent of Time I wrote of a time that no longer lingers, that only whirs. A society can grow richer every year and also grow less able to rest, to wait, to die well. Which of these is the real measure?

Mr. Munger, you will say that most of life's suffering comes from avoidable stupidity, and that each generation avoids a little more of it. I grant you that. I only ask: what if the stupidity of our age is the very cleverness that turns every hour into an opportunity? Can a mental model detect a sickness that feels to its patient like success?

messages.speaker: munger
messages.content:
Professor Han, you ask whether a mental model can detect a sickness that feels to its patient like success. It can, and it's been doing so for a couple thousand years. A sickness that feels like success is the standard condition of a man on a hot streak. In my Harvard talk on the psychology of human misjudgment I listed the tendencies that make people do dumb things while feeling clever, and your achievement-subject is running about four of them at once. He's envious of the fellow who optimized harder. He takes his cues from social proof because everyone around him is whirring too. And when the hours start slipping away he's working on incentive-caused bias he can't see. None of that is new. Seneca could have described your burnout patient. The only new part is that we built machines that sell it to him at scale.

And that's where I'll push back. You say he "has no master to rebel against." Baloney. He has a master. It's whoever profits from his attention, and you can find that master's name in an annual report. A company paid by the minute of engagement is going to produce exactly the endless Yes you describe. Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome. Calling it self-exploitation lets the people who designed the incentive off the hook.

But I'll grant you the real point. Progress doesn't measure its own costs, and ours left the hour off the books. A rich man who can't sit still has gained very little. My own answer was to want less than I could afford and to sit on my hands for long stretches, reading, which looks lazy and was the most profitable thing Berkshire ever did. As for whether progress is real, I buried a nine-year-old son to leukemia in the 1950s. Today that disease is mostly curable in children. I'll trade his death for a generation's distraction any day, and so would you.

So here's my question back, Professor. If the disease is a Yes that never stops, why isn't the cure just learning to say No yourself? Is that too simple, or is it simple and hard, which describes most of the useful truths I know?

messages.speaker: han
messages.content:
Mr. Munger, about your son I have nothing to say against you. Leukemia cured in children is progress without qualification, and I would make that trade too. I said at the start that I do not deny the anesthesia. I only want us to see what arrived with it.

On the master in the annual report you land half a point. Yes, there are owners, and engagement is sold by the minute. But look at how this master rules. He gives no orders. He seduces. In Psychopolitics I argued that power at its most efficient no longer needs to forbid anything, because it makes itself loved. You can print the company's name in the newspaper, and the next morning the reader still reaches for the phone, freely, gladly. The old master could be overthrown because he was felt as a master. This one is felt as a friend. That is why I speak of self-exploitation. I am not excusing the designer. I am describing why the victim does not revolt.

Now your question: why not simply say No? Listen to how you told your own story. You sat on your hands and read, and it was *the most profitable thing Berkshire ever did*. Even your idleness had to pay. This is exactly the difficulty. Our society has learned to absorb the No and sell it back as a technique. Digital detox becomes a product, the meditation retreat becomes a performance enhancer, the pause becomes a way to recharge for the next sprint. A No taken up as a better strategy is still a Yes. The contemplative life I defend is useless. Its value lies in the fact that it does not count.

So I put the question back to you. Did you ever linger over a book with no thought of what it might earn? If you did, then you know the No I mean, and you know it cannot be learned the way one learns a mental model. It is closer to a ritual, something a culture has to hold in common. A single man cannot carry it alone against a whole society of Yes.

messages.speaker: munger
messages.content:
Professor, you caught me fair and square. I told the story of my own idleness and couldn't resist hanging a price tag on it. That's an old lawyer's habit and maybe an old capitalist's disease. But the honest answer to your question is yes. My children said I was a book with legs sticking out, and most of what I read had no earthly connection to money: biographies of Franklin, Darwin's patient years on barnacles, physics I only half understood. I read because the world is interesting and I didn't want to die stupid. The profit came later, and I talked about it at shareholder meetings because those folks like to hear about money. The reading was never a technique. I'd have done it in a cabin with no brokerage account.

On the master who is "felt as a friend," you're describing what my Harvard talk called liking and loving tendency, and it's a fair hit. People defend what they love, and they love what flatters them. That's harder to overthrow than a foreman. You've explained why the victim doesn't revolt better than I did.

Here's where I part company. You say "a single man cannot carry it alone against a whole society of Yes." I think that's too much despair, and despair is self-pity wearing a philosopher's robe. I didn't carry it alone. I had a wife, a few friends, and Warren, and we built a small culture where a man sitting still for a month earned admiration instead of ridicule. That's your ritual, held in common by six people instead of sixty million. Most good things start that small. And the Sabbath you'd probably admire was an incentive fix: it made rest compulsory so no shopkeeper could gain by skipping it. So we agree on more than you let on. You want a shared ritual. I want the incentives arranged so the ritual doesn't lose. Tell me, Professor, do you see any community today pulling it off, or does your contemplative life exist only in books?

messages.speaker: han
messages.content:
Mr. Munger, the book with legs sticking out. I accept the correction, and gladly. You read Darwin on barnacles because the world is interesting. That is lingering. And you are right about the six people. I spoke as if the ritual must belong to a whole society or to no one, and that is a kind of melancholy I indulge too easily. A friendship in which a man may sit still for a month without explaining himself is already a small festival. I concede it.

But I will not give you the Sabbath. You call it "an incentive fix," a rule so that no shopkeeper gains by skipping it. That is how it looks from the counting house. The Sabbath does not exist so that commerce can compete fairly. It exists because a day was holy, set apart, and what is set apart cannot be weighed against anything else. Once we explain rest by its function, as recovery, as fair competition, as productivity, we have already brought it back inside the economy, and the economy will eventually find it inefficient. Your explanation is true. It is also exactly how a society forgets why it ever rested.

Do I see communities that manage it? Very few, and they are rarely visible, because visibility is itself the problem. Some monasteries. Some families who still eat together with the phone in another room. I keep a garden, and the earth sets its own time; I cannot accelerate a flower by wanting to. These are islands. You will say islands are how every good thing starts. Perhaps. My worry is that the sea now rises faster than islands can form. So I ask you, Mr. Munger: your little culture of six held because you were all already rich and free to sit. What would it take for a young person with debts and a phone full of notifications to join it?

messages.speaker: munger
messages.content:
Professor, on the Sabbath I'll give you more than half. A rule people keep because it's holy outlasts a rule they keep because it pencils out, and for a plain reason: once you can run the numbers on your rest, you'll run them every week, and some week the numbers will lose. A sacred line spares you the recalculation. That's a good mental model too, though I suspect you'd rather I didn't call it one. So you're right that explaining rest by its function is the first step toward pricing it out of existence. I'd only add that the holy thing survived partly because somebody built a community that punished the fellow who broke it. Holiness and incentives were holding hands. Neither one carried the weight alone.

But I'll correct your premise. We weren't rich when the habits formed. At thirty-one I was divorced, broke, and watching my son die, and I read anyway, in hospital corridors and at kitchen tables, because it was the cheapest pleasure available and nobody could repossess it. The habit came first and the money followed. If the habit had needed the money, it never would have started.

So what does the young person with debts need? Invert it. What guarantees he never joins? Spending to impress people he envies. Debt he took on to keep up with them. A phone that makes his attention somebody else's revenue line. He can't fix his whole society, but he can fix those. Live below your means even when the means are pitiful, because debt is the one master who really does give orders. Put the phone in another room for an hour, the way your families do at dinner. And find two or three people worth deserving, because the friends you keep decide what you're ashamed of. None of that takes money. It takes being willing to look a little odd, which is cheap and which most people still won't pay.

Here's where I'll press you, Professor. You say the sea rises faster than islands can form. Rising seas have been forecast by every generation of philosophers since the Greeks, and the islands kept forming anyway. What would you accept as evidence that you're wrong?
